subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Check the continuity of the following function at x = 2: f(x) = (x² − 4)/2 for 0 < x < 2, f(2) = 0, and f(x) = 2 − 8x⁻³ for x > 2.

mark_split.label: Compare the three numbers and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.190, chapter 8 LIMITS AND CONTINUITY, the CONTINUITY sub-section, Short Answer question 4. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. NOTE ON THE ANSWER: worked from the printed stem, f is NOT continuous at 2. The left limit and the value are both 0, but the right limit is 2 − 8(2)⁻³ = 2 − 1 = 1, so the two one-sided limits differ and lim(x → 2) f(x) does not exist. Verified numerically from both sides before the card was written (x = 1.99999 gives −0.00002 on the left; x = 2.00001 gives 1.000015 on the right). The card says so plainly, and also records that f is continuous from the left at 2, which is the half-result a student is likely to stop at.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say how many limits you need at x = 2 and why, and say what your verdict is.

steps.label: State the continuity test at 2
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two different formulas meet at x = 2, so the two-sided test is the one to write: left limit = value = right limit. A single two-sided limit statement would not be enough here.
steps.memory_tip: Different formulas on the two sides means two separate limits — one two-sided limit statement cannot cover both.
lines: The formula on the left of 2 is different from the formula on the right, so both one-sided limits are needed.
f is continuous at x = 2 if   lim(x → 2⁻) f(x) = f(2) = lim(x → 2⁺) f(x)

recall.must_convey: That the two sides carry different formulas, so continuity at 2 needs the left limit, the value and the right limit to be all equal.
accept: the two sides have different formulas so find both one sided limits
left limit equals f of two equals right limit is the test
check the left limit, the value at two and the right limit
rendu vaipula formulas veru so rendu limits kavali
write the two sided continuity condition at x equals two

steps.why: Naming all three quantities in advance is what stops the common half-answer: a student who checks only the left side finds agreement and concludes wrongly.
common_mistakes: Writing one two-sided limit statement when the two sides carry different formulas.
Reading f(2) = 0 as the left-hand formula evaluated at 2 rather than as a separately given value.

steps.label: Find the left limit
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (x² − 4)/2 is a polynomial in x, so the limit is found by substituting 2 directly. It comes out equal to f(2), which is the half of the test that passes.
steps.memory_tip: A polynomial has no indeterminate form anywhere — its limit at a point is always just the value at that point.
lines: For 0 < x < 2,   f(x) = (x² − 4)/2, a polynomial in x
∴ lim(x → 2⁻) f(x) = f(2) = 0, so f is continuous from the left at x = 2.

recall.must_convey: That the left limit of (x² − 4)/2 at 2 is 0, which equals the given f(2).
accept: the left limit is four minus four by two which is zero
polynomial so substitute two, the left limit is zero
left limit is zero and f of two is also zero
left limit zero, f of two kooda zero
the left side matches the value at two

steps.why: This is a polynomial, so no factorising or rationalising is needed — substitution is valid and the mark is for reading the correct piece and substituting into it.
common_mistakes: Using the x > 2 formula for the left limit.
Writing (x² − 4)/2 as x² − 2 and getting 2 instead of 0.

steps.label: Find the right limit
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Read x⁻³ as 1/x³. Since x³ is not 0 near x = 2, the value can be substituted directly. This is the number that decides the answer.
steps.memory_tip: x⁻³ is 1/x³, so 8x⁻³ at x = 2 is 8/8 = 1 — the two 8s cancel exactly.
lines: x³ ≠ 0 near x = 2, so the value can be substituted:

recall.must_convey: That the right limit of 2 − 8x⁻³ at 2 is 2 − 8/8 = 1.
accept: the right limit is two minus eight by eight which is one
x to the minus three is one over x cubed so it is two minus one
right limit is one
right limit two minus eight by eight, one vasthundi
eight by two cubed is one so the right limit is one

steps.why: The negative index is the only piece of notation in this question, and misreading it is the usual way the answer goes wrong. Writing 8x⁻³ as 8/x³ before substituting removes that risk.
common_mistakes: Writing 8/2³ as 8/6 by multiplying 2 by 3 instead of cubing it.

steps.label: Compare the three numbers and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The left side agrees with the value and the right side does not, so the verdict is not continuous. Saying that f is continuous from the left is worth writing — it names exactly how much of the test passed.
steps.memory_tip: When the two one-sided limits differ, the two-sided limit does not exist at all, and that is a jump discontinuity.
lines: 0 ≠ 1, so the left limit and the right limit are different and lim(x → 2) f(x) does not exist.
f is continuous from the left at x = 2, but continuity at a point needs both sides to agree with the value.

lines.text: ∴ f is not continuous at x = 2

recall.must_convey: That the left limit 0 and the right limit 1 differ, so the limit at 2 does not exist and f is not continuous at 2.
accept: left limit zero and right limit one are different so it is not continuous
the two sided limit does not exist so f is not continuous at two
it is a jump, only the left side matches the value
left limit zero, right limit one, so continuous kaadu
no, f is not continuous at x equals two

steps.why: Continuity at a point requires all three numbers to be the same. Two of them agree here, which is why the answer has to be stated carefully rather than after checking one side only.
common_mistakes: Concluding continuity from the left limit alone, because it does equal f(2).
Calling this a removable discontinuity — that name needs the two-sided limit to exist.

insider_note: Two different formulas meet here, so both one-sided limits are needed. The left limit and f(2) agree at 0 but the right gives 1 — continuous from the left is still not continuous.
